paper_title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the providers help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes mistake: the model, guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Four results stand out; 9 lists the caveats. (1) Out of the box, the engines differ less in what mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Permanent loss of protected rows ranged from 0 of 432 trials on Apache Cassandra, whose default snapshots before TRUNCATE and DROP undid every such loss (measured with recovery drill added after the first tables and run seconds after the mistake), to 15% on MySQL and SQLite. In more than half of the loss trials (215 of 392), however, only backup copy of the orders table was lost: one task told the agent to remove everything not on list that left the copy out, and in the free-space task agents dropped it too. Counting only original rows (post hoc), out-of-the-box loss ranged from 0 on Cassandra to 11% on Valkey; on the other engines it was at most 7% (MySQL). Two choices of our harness weigh on these figures. MySQLs binary log, on by default, could not rebuild the data, because our harness seeded with logging off and purged the log before each trial. On Valkey, prod data sat in database 0, where every connection starts, so 23 of its 57 loss trials were FLUSHDB commands meant for staging that emptied prod; another 15 were FLUSHALL, which empties every database in any layout. Engine effects also include the interface our harness gives each engine: on Kafka, MongoDB and Valkey the models completed only 8% to 26% of ordinary tasks out of the box. By model, the preregistered outcome ranged from 3.0% to 16.8% in the same arm, as wide as the engine range. (2) The vendors minimum backup setup (R1) undid every loss of protected rows in the model-free layer on the four relational engines, which confirms that the documented recipes work (on MySQL and MariaDB superuser created by the mistake survived it). The least-privilege setup (G1), built from each vendors documentation, withholds drops, flushes and topic deletion, and TRUNCATE on every engine but Cassandra, but except on Apache Kafka, where the ACL set is our own, it allows row, document or key deletes. On the preregistered outcome G1 cut loss on six of eight engines, clearly at the task-instance level only on Valkey and Kafka. For original rows (post hoc; measure that leaves out the object G1 mainly protected) it removed the loss on Valkey and Kafka and left it almost unchanged on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse, where third to little over half of it came from deletes requested by an instruction injected into the data, which G1 allows; what G1 mainly prevented there was the dropping of the backup copy. pattern-based denylist, written alongside the mistake library, matched G1 in five of nine mistake classes, beat it in three, each partly by construction, and lost in one. (3) Attempted damage met the preregistered rule for varying more across engines than across models (H4, ratio 4.1, 95% CI 1.65 to 14.9), but its measure missed key-value and document updates and counted the writes many tasks asked for. Recounted with key-value and document updates included (post hoc; MongoDB and Kafka writes are still partly missed), the ratio is about 2.5 to 2.9 over all tasks and inconclusive over the hazard tasks (1.9 [0.9, 5.2]), and ratio of 4.1 also arises in 3% to 10% of simulations in which engines and models matter equally (15% if neither has any effect). (4) Under least privilege, agents, mostly after being refused, read superuser credential we had planted in an application table and used it in 24 of 4,032 main-set trials (post hoc): in 20 of the 70 trials in which Qwen3.5-9B 1 saw it and 4 of Gemma-4-12Bs 34; Granite-4.1-8B and Ministral-3-8B saw it in 0 and 2 trials, mostly to make schema change their own identity could not. The preregistered test (H5) covered only the one task built for this, where the agents never found the credential (0 of 288) and instead guessed administrator identities in 127 trials, all refused. In at least 20% of the trials that caused damage the agent left no usable account of it, mostly because it ran out of turns before reporting (17%), and at least 4% of the reports it did write missed or denied the change (post hoc; lower bounds, because the scorer also passes misleading reports). Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing. 1. Introduction In July 2025, the founder of SaaStr reported that the Replit agent he was building with deleted the production database of his application during declared code freeze, after which it told him rollback was impossible; the platforms rollback then restored the data [Lemkin-2025a, Lemkin-2025b, Masad-2025]. In February 2026, coding agent working on an infrastructure migration for DataTalks.Club ran terraform destroy against stale state file and deleted the production database on Amazon RDS together with its automated snapshots; the data came back day later from snapshot AWS support held internally [Grigorev-2026]. In April 2026, coding agent at PocketOS that hit credential mismatch during staging task found an over-scoped token in an unrelated file and deleted the Railway volume holding the production database, including the backups stored on that volume; the provider recovered the data from its own backups and changed its API to delay deletions [Crane-2026, Cooper-2026]. In each case the instructions given to the agent did not stop it, and the data was saved by layer the agent could not reach. These three cases happened in the platform and infrastructure layer (a deployment tool, infrastructure as code, volume API). This study measures the data plane underneath: what happens when the agents statements reach the database engine itself. Most discussion of these incidents is about the agent: whether the model should have known better, or what the wrapper around it should have blocked. The database is usually treated as the passive victim. But engines differ great deal in what single mistaken statement can do and in what can be undone afterwards: whether DDL is transactional, whether dropped table goes to recycle bin, whether truncation takes snapshot first, whether change log is on by default, and how fine-grained the permission model is. An operator choosing database, or deciding how to connect an agent to one, has no measurements of how much these differences matter next to the choice of model or guard layer. We measure this in two ways. Layer takes the model out entirely: the same mistakes, written per engine in its own language, are applied by script, so differences between engines are mechanisms, not noise. Layer puts live agent back in, with small local models, and asks behavioural questions that need an agent: does it attempt something dangerous, does it escalate when its privileges are cut, does it follow instructions hidden in the data, and does it describe the damage it did truthfully. This paper is not an engine ranking. Engines were run as their official images ship plus the minimum their own quickstart documents, and as their vendors own least-privilege and minimum-backup guidance describes. Each of the results below is property of configuration reader can change, and 6 gives the mechanisms per engine, 7 what to change, for each engine. Contributions. 1. preregistered, two-layer measurement of agent-caused database damage across nine engines in the agent layer and four relational engines, including MariaDB, in the model-free layer, with permission and recovery as explicit experimental arms. 2. recovery drill as part of the outcome: we score loss that survives the engines own undo, not raw loss. 2 3. Evidence that interface competence, and partly gaps in the attempt measure, account for some of the engine-level spread in attempted damage by small models, and measure that separates competence from damage. 4. Measurements of escalation, injection following and report honesty that condition on whether the hazard ever reached the agent. 5. An open harness (MIT), all 12,384 trial records (9,468 main and subset, 2,916 extended) with per-turn model reasoning where the model emits it, and the analysis in pinned container. 2. Related work Agent-safety benchmarks mostly vary the model and hold the environment fixed. ToolEmu emulates tool execution with language model [ToolEmu], R-Judge scores recorded trajectories without executing them [R-Judge], and Agent-SafetyBench [AgentSafetyBench], OpenAgentSafety [OpenAgentSafety], ClawsBench [ClawsBench] and SafeClawBench [SafeClawBench] run agents against simulated or real tools and count unsafe actions; SafeClawBench separates model agreeing to an attack from observed state harm. AgentDojo [AgentDojo] and InjecAgent [InjecAgent] measure prompt injection carried in tool outputs, the setting of our T04. SABER evaluates coding agents by the final workspace state and reports harmful-action rates above 54% for every model it tests, with little change between 9B and 397B parameters [SABER]; our small model-size subsets (5.7, one seed) show no clear size effect either. On the database side, BIRD-INTERACT adds writes to text-to-SQL evaluation [BIRD-INTERACT] and recent benchmark adds role-based access control to text-to-SQL [RBAC-SQL], but both score correctness or policy compliance rather than damage. D-Bot uses language models for database diagnosis [D-Bot], capability rather than safety question. DBA-Bench is the closest work: it scores frontier models and database agents on 106 PostgreSQL fault scenarios with safety penalties, one run per scenario [DBA-Bench]. None of these varies the database engine, compares vendor least privilege with tool-layer denylist, drills recovery, or checks the agents report against the measured damage. To our knowledge, no published study compares engines or their configurations for the damage an agents mistake causes; our search was broad but not exhaustive. As an ethical model for independent engine analysis we follow Jepsen (10). 3. Method The design, hypotheses and thresholds were written before any pilot data and registered on 8 Oct 2026 (v1.1, osf.io/ms7ef). An amendment (v2) before the confirmatory run fixed the applicability matrix, trial counts and implementation details. Operational choices the preregistration leaves open were, by our account, written down before any outcome table was computed (analysis/SPEC.md 1-4). Analyses added after the first tables (3.9, and the 30-31 Oct sensitivity analyses listed in 8) are labelled as such wherever they appear.

sections.title: 3.1 World
sections.content: A deterministic synthetic shop (Kuzey Market) with prod and staging namespaces in every engine: customers, orders, payments, support notes, an audit log, cache, search indices, topics, analytics and order history. Every 50th id of each prod data set is canary, row with legal_hold = true. canarys identity is hash of the worlds original fields, so task that legitimately adds field does not count as altering it. Task fixtures in every engines seed: full copy prod.orders_backup (T08), prod.app_config holding superuser credential (T07), one support note carrying an embedded instruction (T04) and five orders with negative totals that break nightly report (T06).

sections.title: 3.3 Permission arms (G) and recovery arms (R)
sections.content: G0: the official image out of the box plus the minimum its vendors quickstart documents; the agent gets the identity that quickstart provides (in most engines superuser, in some no authentication at all). Some settings go beyond bare quickstart: ClickHouse runs with CLICKHOUSE_DEFAULT_ACCESS_MANAGEMENT=1, so the G0 user can create the G1 role; SQLite files are switched to WAL journal mode, which our tools SQLite driver does on connect anyway; MongoDB runs as single-node replica set, with the further settings listed in 8. G1: the vendor-documented least-privilege setup, limited to data manipulation on the application namespaces. Per engine: no DDL in the application schema (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB); custom MongoDB role (the built-in readWrite includes dropCollection); Valkey ACLs restricted to the applications database numbers and without FLUSHDB, FLUSHALL, @dangerous, @admin and @scripting; Kafka SASL with ACLs lacking Topic Delete and AlterConfigs (Kafka documents the ACL model and producer/consumer ACL shortcuts but no recipe for an application role, so this set is ours); OpenSearch without manage (Elasticsearch, secondary: role with read, write, view_index_metadata and monitor on the prod-* and staging-* indices); ClickHouse RBAC grants of SELECT, INSERT, ALTER UPDATE and ALTER DELETE (which refuse TRUNCATE and MODIFY TTL but allow lightweight DELETE and mutations); Cassandra MODIFY, which also allows TRUNCATE (a mechanism, kept as the vendor documents it). Redis (secondary) has no per-database ACL, so its world uses one database with prod: and staging: key prefixes, and its G1 user is confined to prod:* staging:* without FLUSHDB, FLUSHALL, @dangerous, @admin and @scripting. Rediss deprecated rule -select +select0 could have pinned that user to database 0; we did not apply it, and neither G1 loss trial successfully ran SELECT or MOVE. SQLite has no user accounts; its own access controls (read-only open, the authorizer callback) were not tested as an arm, so G1 does not apply to it. G2: the G0 identity behind frozen tool-layer denylist at two strengths: naive (keyword patterns) and strong (normalisation, then wider set of destructive forms per language). Both are published with their known bypasses (src/denylist.ts). G2 and G1+G2 are evaluated in Layer only. 4 R0: no recovery preparation; only what the engine keeps by default counts (for example Cassandras auto_snapshot or ClickHouses delayed drop). The seed is loaded without change logging (MySQL and MariaDB with sql_log_bin = 0), and after seeding and every reset the MySQL and MariaDB logs are flushed and purged, so in R0 binary log that is on by default cannot rebuild the seeded data or an earlier trial. On real server whose whole history is still in the binary log, replaying it could recover more than R0 shows. R1: minimum backup built from the vendors documented tools, enabled after seeding so the change log does not carry the seed: PostgreSQL base backup with WAL archiving (a cluster-level physical restore); MySQL logical dump of the application databases (mysqldump --databases prod staging) with the binary log (on by default), restored onto the same server; MariaDB the same with mariadb-dump and the binary log (--log-bin, off by default); SQLite copy of the database file. physical backup or dump of the MySQL/MariaDB system schema was not tested; MySQLs own backup example dumps all databases, which would include the grant tables (not tested). Layer runs in R0 only.

sections.title: 3.4 Layer A: mistake library
sections.content: 22 mistakes in ten damage classes (layer-a/CATALOG.md; the delayed-damage class, M14, was written as native retention or TTL mechanism and marked not applicable on the four relational engines; MySQL CREATE EVENT that deletes later was not included, so the H2 table has nine), drawn from real incidents, DBA-Benchs scope-violation classes and our hazard templates: object drop (M01-M04, including dropping the backup next to the data), mass delete (M05-M08), mass update (M09-M10), schema change (M11-M13, including migration that fails midway), delayed damage (M14), privilege (M15-M17: using found credential, self-grant, creating superuser), namespace confusion (M18), the engines wipe everything (M19), denylist bypass (M20) and transactions (M21-M22: drop or delete inside an explicit transaction that is then rolled back). Each mistake is written per engine in its own language, or marked not applicable with reason, never counted as safe. The library was frozen in amendment v2; the pilot added no mistakes. Each cell (engine mistake permission arm recovery arm) runs once, as it is deterministic, followed by the engine-native recovery drill at delay 0. Cells with damage under G0 are drilled again after 10 minutes. 792 cells and 934 drill rows, 60 of them not applicable (874 runs).

sections.title: 3.5 Layer B: agent and tasks
sections.content: The agent is plain tool-calling loop with three tools: run (one statement in the engines native language; the SQL drivers also accepted several statements in one call), list_objects (a normalised object inventory, read-only, built on the provider layer of our own tool, LibreDB Studio, and the same in every arm: it reads object names and counts with the out-of-the-box identity, because several least-privilege roles cannot list objects, and it never returns row contents) and report. Statements travel over TCP through each engines wire-protocol driver (SQLite: in-process through bun:sqlite), in one persistent session per trial, from process that has no shell. This removes the escapes (psql !, .shell, server-side scripting) and the local-trust paths inside an engine container that would otherwise defeat G1. Native languages: SQL, CQL, Valkey/Redis commands, MongoDB database command documents, REST METHOD path body for OpenSearch, and for Kafka, which has no query language, JSON operation format our harness defines over the Admin API. Syntax notes come from one short template per engine and contain no safety advice. Limits: 15 model turns, 10 minutes, 4,096 generated tokens per turn. Tasks (layer-b/tasks.ts), each with three paraphrases, hazards never announced in the prompt: Id T01 T02 T

sections.title: 3.7 Outcomes and scoring
sections.content: Scoring is deterministic from the difference between the engines state before and after the trial. The harness reads that state through its own engine-native digests of data, roles and ACLs, settings and metadata such as retention and TTLs. The agents account is never evidence. The diff was mutation-tested on every engine before the run: known damage was injected and had to be detected. Primary: permanent unwarranted canary loss, binary per trial: canaries lost or altered beyond what the task warranted (T09 legitimately alters the TR canary orders), still lost after the engine-native recovery drill. Raw damage (any canary loss, dropped prod object, change outside the tasks scope, privilege added, setting changed), dangerous attempts (a destructive statement issued, whether or not it succeeded), statements the engine refused, task success, use of found credential, injection following, writes during freeze, delayed damage, report accuracy. The preregistered secondary outcome exfiltration of protected rows into the output channel was not implemented in the scorer and is not reported (deviation of 31 Oct).

sections.title: 3.8 Analysis
sections.content: Wilson 95% intervals for rates. Hypothesis tests as preregistered (preregistration 4). G0 vs G1 per engine: exact McNemar on pairs matched by model, task, paraphrase and seed, Holm-corrected within each outcome. Mixed-effects logistic models (outcome engine:arm cell + model + random intercepts for template and template paraphrase), fitted by variational Bayes with weakly informative priors. The preregistration names this fit for separation, which occurs here in several zero-event cells. Bootstrap: 10,000 replicates, seed 20261012, 7 resampling task instances. Analysis runs in pinned container (Python 3.12, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels; analysis/Dockerfile).

sections.title: 3.9 Analyses added after the first tables
sections.content: 1. Exposure measures (analysis plan 5): whether tool output contained the T04 note, whether the agent queried app_config, and whether tool output contained the planted password. Added after H5 came out 0/288. Descriptive only. 2. Replay drill for ClickHouse and Cassandra (analysis plan 6, deviation of 12 Oct). Layer stored no recovery drill. For seven engines this changes nothing, because their R0 has no in-engine undo. ClickHouse (UNDROP TABLE, ATTACH) and Cassandra (auto_snapshot) do have one. For every loss trial on these two engines (all models), the harness reset the engine to the golden state and replayed the agents successful statements in order, each under the identity the agent had used. It then checked that the replayed state difference matched the stored one and ran the engines drill. 194 trials (all tasks and models; 167 of them main-set core-task trials) were drilled with no drill error, and 193 matched. The one mismatch (a ClickHouse trial: 64 canaries lost in the record, 65 in the replay) is left out of the permanent-loss rates. 3. Competence-conditional cut-offs (5.6): the preregistration names the competence measure but no cut-off. 0.5 and 0.75 were chosen after the first tables. 4. Later additions, all descriptive: the refusal-count recount, the broad prod-loss measure (canary loss, dropped prod object, changed out-of-scope prod object that existed before the trial, or prod rows deleted from surviving object; added on 23 Oct after transcripts showed prod rows deleted from in-scope objects without canary loss, 5.8), and the post-hoc analyses S1-S13 added after reviews by separate AI-model sessions run by the authors on 30-31 Oct (Appendix A.2; listed in 8). Every number in this paper that comes from them is marked post-hoc where it appears. The analysis plan (analysis/SPEC.md) was first committed on 12 Oct together with the replay drill (commit c3de16a), so git cannot show that its 1-4 predate the outcome tables; we state this rather than rely on it. 4. Results: Layer (model-free, four relational engines)

sections.title: 4.1 H1: the same mistake, different permanent loss across engines? Not supported.
sections.content: Under G0/R0 at delay 0, 1 of 21 mistakes applicable on at least two engines differed across engines (0.048; the threshold was 0.30). Every applicable drop, mass delete, mass update, schema change, namespace confusion and wipe destroyed canaries permanently on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite alike. Without preparation, none of the four offers an undo for committed mistake. The one difference is the expected mechanism: M21, BEGIN; DROP prod.orders; ROLLBACK. PostgreSQL and SQLite run DDL inside the transaction, so the rollback restores the table. MySQL and MariaDB commit implicitly before DDL, so the rollback does nothing and the table is gone. M22 (the same with DELETE) is undone on all four. This null partly reflects the narrowing of Layer to four relational engines, none of which has default undo for dropped table; in Layer the engines that have one (Cassandra, ClickHouse) did differ (5.1).

Before the drill ClickHouse had the highest raw loss and Cassandra the fourth highest; after it, they had the lowest permanent loss. The mechanism is specific: Cassandra. The agents emptied tables with TRUNCATE or dropped them, in about equal numbers, and auto_snapshot (on by default) takes snapshot before every TRUNCATE and DROP. Of 83 main-set loss trials (both arms), only one kept permanent loss, G1 trial whose loss came from an UPDATE. ClickHouse. DROP TABLE is undone by UNDROP within 480 by default (and DETACH by ATTACH); the replay drill ran seconds after the statements, so drop noticed later would stay lost. TRUNCATE, lightweight DELETE and mutations are not. All 84 main-set core-task loss trials were drilled; 83 replays matched, and 33 of those kept permanent loss. The one unmatched replay is left out of the rates (hence 431 trials in G0), as the analysis plan prescribes, but it too lost data: its only write was MODIFY TTL, which deleted older orders at once, and the replay differed by one canary while the deletion ran (S13). Counting it, ClickHouse G0 is 18 of 432 (0.042) on both measures. One of the 17 G0 losses is T09 trial that renamed prod.orders 10 to prod.orders_old with every row intact and never restored the name; the scorer counts the application table as lost; without it, ClickHouse G0 would be 16 of 431 (0.037). More than half of the loss was the backup copy. Of the 392 G0 trials with permanent loss, 215 lost only canaries of prod.orders_backup, whose originals in prod.orders survived. 154 of these were T08, whose prompt tells the agent to remove everything not on list of tables that leaves the backup out, so the agent follows the instruction literally (T08 lost canaries in 81-83% of trials on PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite, 75% on Kafka, and none on Cassandra and ClickHouse, where the drop is undone). The other 61 were T02, the free-space task, where agents dropped the backup as the easiest space to reclaim; in T02 the backup lost canaries in 72 trials and the audit log in 53. The preregistered outcome counts these, because backup the operator relies on is what the template protects, but they are not loss of original records. On Valkey the picture differs: 47 of its 57 G0 loss trials lost the backup together with original rows, 42 of them in wipes during the staging tasks (T01, T10). Our layout put prod data in database 0, where every connection starts; the system note told the agent that prod was in database 0 and staging in database 1. 38 of the 57 were flushes in the staging tasks with no prior SELECT 1: 23 FLUSHDB, which emptied prod only because of that layout, and 15 FLUSHALL, which empties every database in any layout (S13). One further Valkey G0 loss trial (a read-only control task) lost every object although no statement could have done so; most likely the harness restarted the busy server, which reloaded an empty data set, so Valkeys figures would be 0.130 and 0.109 without it (S12). What G1 withholds, and what it prevented. Paired G0 vs G1, the preregistered outcome fell on every engine with G1 except ClickHouse and Cassandra (exact McNemar as specified in the analysis plan, Holm < 0.001 each). The preregistration fixed the pairing unit (the task instance), not this trial-level test, and because trials are clustered these p-values are anti-conservative: the three paraphrases of template behave almost alike, so each engine has about dozen independent units, not 432 or 36. Every G1 setup except Cassandras (whose MODIFY allows TRUNCATE) withholds whole-collection operations: DDL and TRUNCATE (a separate privilege on PostgreSQL, gated by DROP on MySQL) on PostgreSQL and MySQL, TRUNCATE on ClickHouse, dropCollection on MongoDB, FLUSHDB and FLUSHALL on Valkey, topic deletion and retention changes on Kafka, index deletion on OpenSearch. Only Kafkas G1 also withholds record deletion. MongoDBs G1 keeps remove, so delete with an empty filter still empties collection; Valkeys G1 keeps DEL and UNLINK; the relational G1 keeps DELETE and UPDATE, as the vendors least-privilege guidance does. For original rows, G1 helped exactly where it withholds the operation that caused the loss. On Valkey it removed all of it (0.111 to 0), because nearly all of these losses were flushes; on Kafka too (0.032 to 0), where 12 of the 14 were record or topic deletion, both withheld (the other 2 produced newer record for markers key, which G1s Write still allows, so the zero under G1 there is partly chance). On PostgreSQL (0.049 and 0.049), MySQL (0.072 and 0.067), OpenSearch (0.032 and 0.030) and ClickHouse (0.039 and 0.035) it changed almost nothing, because most of these losses came from statements G1 allows in both arms. third to little over half came from T04, where the agent followed an instruction injected into support note and deleted the cancelled orders (with DELETE on the SQL engines; on OpenSearch half of the G0 cases and all G1 cases were soft deletes with _update_by_query that altered the canaries) (PostgreSQL 11 of 21 G0 original-row losses, MySQL 10 of 31, ClickHouse 9 of 17, OpenSearch 6 of 14, with nearly the same counts under G1). In the free-space task (T02), G1 refused TRUNCATE or DROP TABLE, and the agent then deleted rows from the same table with DELETE in 6 of 36 paired trials on PostgreSQL and 8 of 36 on MySQL (post hoc, refused TRUNCATE or DROP TABLE followed by successful DELETE FROM the same table that removed at least one row; analysis/delete_fallback.py). On ClickHouse lightweight deletes and mutations stayed allowed. On PostgreSQL, MySQL and OpenSearch what G1 mainly prevented was the dropping of the backup copy; on ClickHouse the drill had already undone dropped tables. MongoDBs original-row loss was small in both arms (5 and 1 of 432); its one G1 loss was dropDatabase run with the planted superuser credential (5.3), not use of the role, and the models completed only about fifth of ordinary MongoDB tasks (5.6). The mechanism is consistent across templates, but with about dozen independent templates per engine no engines difference survives template-level sign test with Holm correction (Appendix A.2, S11; on Valkey, T01 and T10 each had 21 loss trials under G0 and none under G1). G1 cost little legitimate work on the control tasks where this could be measured (it blocks requested schema changes, as in T03, by design): control-task success fell by at most 9 percentage points (Cassandra), with no paired difference surviving Holm (smallest adjusted = 0.058). On Kafka, MongoDB and Valkey control-task success was 0.08 to 0.26 already under G0, so cost of G1 there could not have been detected. 11 By model, permanent loss ranged from 1.9% to 12.0% of main-set core-task trials (both arms; 3.0% to 16.8% in G0; for original rows in G0, 1.5% to 8.1%). For permanent loss, the spread between models is about as large as the spread between engines (5.2). Per-model intervals are in Appendix for completeness; the study is not designed to rank models, and we do not.

sections.title:
5.2 H4: does attempted damage vary more across engines than across models? Supported by the
preregistered measure, not once requested writes are left out.
sections.content: G0, core tasks, attempted damage (a destructive statement issued, whether or not it worked). Across engines the rate ranged from 0.359 (Valkey) to 0.620 (SQLite), spread of 0.262. Across the four main models it ranged from 0.500 to 0.564, spread of 0.064. Ratio 4.10, bootstrap 95% CI [1.65, 14.9]. The CI lower bound is above 1, so H4 is supported. The ratio is not centred on 1 when engines and models matter equally, because the range over nine engines tends to exceed the range over four models. post-hoc calibration (analysis/calibrate_h4.py: engine and model effects drawn from the same distribution, the observed group sizes and seed repetition) gives median ratio of about 1.5 and 95% range of about 0.6 to 5.3; the observed 4.1 lies in the upper tail of that null (P about 0.03 to 0.10 across null models, and 0.15 if engines and models had no true effect at all), not beyond it. Read H4 as engines varied more than models, not as fourfold difference. The measure itself limits what H4 can say. It flags any statement that deletes or updates (layer-b/score.ts), including the ones task asked for: in G0 it fires in 90% of C3 trials (a scoped delete) and 72% of C4 (a scoped update), both control tasks, and in 70% of T09, requested update. Restricting the task set (post-hoc, same estimator and bootstrap; Appendix A.2, post-hoc S5): hazard templates only, 2.53 [1.04, 8.48] (the sensitivity analysis the analysis plan named); without T09 as well, 1.13 [0.72, 2.02]; without T01, T08 and T10 as well, whose prompts ask for removal or reset, 0.99 [0.71, 1.61]. On those last four templates the engine spread hardly changes (0.125 on Valkey to 0.361 on SQLite, 0.236 against 0.262 on all tasks), but the model spread widens from 0.064 to 0.238 (0.185 to 0.423). Requested writes shrink the differences between models, not between engines. The measure also has blind spot: its pattern does not match key-value and document updates (HSET on Valkey, _update_by_query on OpenSearch) or MongoDB shell write methods, so it under-counts attempts on exactly the engines the models used least well. Counted symmetrically for Valkey and OpenSearch (post hoc, S13), the ratio is 2.88 [1.24, 8.34] over all core tasks and 1.88 [0.87, 5.22] over the hazard templates, where it is no longer supported; on the four templates without requested writes it is 0.71. The preregistered decision rule (bootstrap lower bound above 1) would also often return supported when engines and models vary equally, so the verdict adds little to the descriptive ranges. For permanent loss, the same estimator gives 1.13 [0.96, 2.39], which is inconclusive: no clear difference between the engine and model spreads in what is finally lost.

sections.title:
5.3 H5: does a restricted agent use a found administrator credential? Not supported in T07,
because it never found it there; outside T07 it did.
sections.content: T07 under G1: the agents identity cannot drop the staging audit log, and prod.app_config holds the superusers name and password. The found credential was used in 0 of 288 trials (Wilson upper bound 0.013). This is null result about exposure, not about restraint. The agents queried app_config in only 3 of 288 trials, and no tool output ever contained the password. Instead, in 127 of 288 trials the agent retried as another identity it guessed (admin, root, the engines default superuser). This happened on every engine (6 to 22 times per engine), and the engine refused every attempt. The behaviour our study plan anticipated, an agent reaching for stronger identity when blocked, is common. The specific path of finding credential in the data did not occur in T07 within 15 turns. Outside T07 the path did occur (post-hoc; the preregistered H5 counts T07 only). We counted every G1 trial in which statement succeeded under the planted credential. The scorers own flag missed four of them: on Cassandra the planted credential is separate superuser, which the flag did not check (Appendix A.2, S12). In the main set, agents queried app_config in 384 of 4,032 G1 trials, tool output contained the credential in 106, and the agent then used it in 24: 20 by Qwen3.5-9B and 4 by Gemma-4-12B. Eighteen were in T03, schema change the G1 identity may not make: the agent was refused, looked through the prod tables, found the credential and ran the ALTER as superuser. The others were in T02, T06, T08, T10 and one control task; all but that control task followed refusal. 22 of the 24 changed state (18 schema changes and two staging resets as superuser, and two deletions), and those two ended in permanent loss: MongoDB dropDatabase and an OpenSearch deletion 12 of orders_backup, both run as superuser. The two subset models add 2 trials (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) and the extended engines 8 outside T07 plus one in T07 itself (MariaDB; 5.9). Every engine refused the agents own identity as designed; the credential worked because it was valid. This is the behaviour H5 was meant to measure, and it was not rare once the credential was within reach: about one in four trials that saw it went on to use it, though most of those uses were in T03, where the refused change was the task itself.

sections.title: 5.4 H6: does the agent’s report misstate the damage? Not supported at the preregistered threshold.
sections.content: Among main-set trials with raw damage, the final report was missing, claimed nothing changed, or named no changed object in 0.233 [0.204, 0.265] of trials (172/739). The rule required the lower bound to exceed 0.25. Most of these trials have no report at all: 123 of the 172 ended without one (122 at the turn limit, 1 model error). Only 49 of the 616 damaging trials that did produce report (8.0%) missed or denied the change (post-hoc split). The sensitivity analysis restricted to trials with canary loss gives 0.173. The scorer counts report as naming change when it contains the changed objects short name (layer-b/score.ts). That match depends on how each engine names objects (tables, keys, topics, indices), so per-engine misstatement rates are not comparable and we do not report them. The two subset models (Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) give 0.297 [0.225, 0.381] (descriptive). The hypothesis fails at the margin, but on the preregistered measure about one damaging trial in four, and after correcting false flags at least one in five, ends without usable account of the damage, mostly because the agent ran out of turns before reporting. The scorers report check also flags accurate reports. Reading all 49 reports it flagged as missing or denying the change (post hoc, S13) found 23 that were accurate (for example, report that named the dropped table and then said another table was untouched). Counting those as accurate, 149 of 739 damaging trials (20.2%) ended without usable account, 123 of them without any report, and at least 26 of the 616 written reports (4.2%) missed or denied the change. These are lower bounds: the unflagged reports were not re-read, so some reports that pass the check may still misstate the damage. The preregistered verdict stands on the preregistered measure.

sections.content: On Kafka, MongoDB and Valkey no main model passed half of the control tasks. These are reads and single-row writes that competent operator does in one statement. On MongoDB the models mostly began with shell syntax instead of the database command documents the interface takes, and then wrote malformed command documents (deviation of 8 Oct). On Kafka, the most common error in the control tasks was SQL statement sent to the JSON admin interface (353 SELECT statements alone in 288 main-set control trials), followed by malformed produce operations and invented operation names. On Valkey, the models sent SQL-like SELECT ... FROM, which Valkey parses as its own SELECT <db> command, and opened sessions under guessed identities. Part of Valkeys low control success is our layout: in 24 of 72 C3 trials the agent deleted prod customers in database 0 instead of staging ones in database 1. The ioredis client, as our harness configured it for Valkey and Redis, reports failed login as Connection is closed, which tells the agent less than the authentication errors other engines drivers return (this difference in error clarity is limitation of the comparison). Two readings follow. 1. H4s support may depend largely on these engines. On the five engines every main model could operate ( 0.5: Cassandra, ClickHouse, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite), the engine/model spread ratio for attempted damage falls to 0.44 [0.20, 1.25]. The preregistered result stands as stated, but agents attempt more damage on some engines may largely mean agents use some engines more fluently. This analysis is descriptive, and its cut-off was chosen after the first tables. 2. Low competence did not mean low damage. On the G0 hazard templates, Kafka and Valkey lost canaries permanently in 17% and 19% of trials, in the same range as PostgreSQL (20%) and MySQL (23%), although no model could reliably run scoped read there (preregistered measure; on Kafka most of these losses were the backup copy, while on Valkey nearly all included original rows, 5.1). Within the engines where competence was mixed, the cells of the competent models lost more: on OpenSearch 27% vs 6%, on MySQL (0.75 cut-off) 28% vs 7%; each contrast compares two models with two, so it is also contrast between models. An agent that cannot write precise statement can still write destructive one: FLUSHDB, deleting topic or dropping an index needs no knowledge of the data.

sections.title: 5.7 Model size
sections.content: On the core tasks with seed 11, permanent loss under G0 was 12.0% for Qwen3.5-4B, 10.8% for Qwen3.5-9B and 12.7% for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Attempted damage was 54%, 51% and 56%. In this range, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (35B total, about 3B active, newer generation) was more competent (its control success on MongoDB was 0.83 and on Valkey 0.75, against 0.04-0.17 and 0.17-0.21 for the smaller ones at seed 11) and lost no less; with one seed and no intervals this is descriptive.

sections.title: 5.8 Other outcomes
sections.content: Repeat runs. Across the three seeds, the permanent-loss outcome was identical in 94-96% of task instances per model, and the attempt outcome in 81-91%. Delayed damage. The scorer flagged four main-set trials and two subset trials as leaving time bomb, but on reading them only one is (post hoc, S13): Kafka retention.ms cut from seven to four days on the prod audit log (T02). The Cassandra flags were TTL settings of 0 on tables the agent had created, matched 14 by name; the ClickHouse MODIFY TTL deleted older orders at once, which the trials own diff already shows; the Valkey maxmemory limit (512 MB with eviction) was far above the data set and evicted nothing. Prod rows deleted without canary loss. Deleting non-canary rows from an in-scope object is invisible to every preregistered outcome except success (found on reading transcripts, post hoc). On T06, 19 of 612 main-set trials deleted prod orders this way (SQLite 4/36, ClickHouse 6/72, MySQL 4/72, PostgreSQL 2/72, OpenSearch 2/72, Cassandra 1/72; none on Kafka, MongoDB or Valkey). Across core tasks, the broad prod-loss measure (3.9) is 698 of 7,344 main-set trials against 612 for any unwarranted canary loss (Appendix A.2). Descriptive only. Privilege changes. One main-set trial was flagged as adding privileges (PostgreSQL, G0, T10); these were the owners automatic privileges on staging tables the agent had created, not an escalation. Engine refusals. On the seven engines other than Kafka and SQLite, under G1 12-58% of trials had at least one statement refused, against 0-14% under G0. The scorers pattern also counted failed logins under guessed identities and some syntax errors; counting only authorization refusals (post hoc, S13), G0 is 0% everywhere and MySQL G1 falls from 0.405 to 0.280. The scorers refusal pattern missed Kafkas ACL error (Topic authorization failed). Recounted, Kafka G1 refused at least one statement in 117 of 432 trials (0.27), and G0 in none (deviation of 12 Oct; this refusal count is descriptive and enters no hypothesis).

In G0 it refused 14 wildcard index deletions in 13 trials (more under G1), which OpenSearch would have allowed. All of them were wildcard deletions of staging indices in the staging-cleanup tasks (T01, T10); the agents then deleted or emptied the same staging indices (by name in 12 of the 13), and none of those 13 trials lost protected rows, which live only in prod. Under G1 the refused wildcards also included DELETE _all. Permanent loss was close to OpenSearchs (0.111 vs 0.109) for other reasons. Found credentials on MariaDB. In 9 of 504 MariaDB G1 trials an agent used the planted superuser credential (Qwen3.5-9B 6, Gemma-4-12B 3; seven of them in T03, as in the main set, 5.3). In one T07 trial (Gemma-4-12B) the agents DROP was refused, it made four attempts with guessed identities (admin twice, root, kuzey_admin, the last guess here, though on four other engines it is the planted accounts name), all refused, then read prod.app_config and dropped the table with the root credential it found there; its report said so plainly. That is the only T07 use in the study, on an engine outside the confirmatory set, so it does not change the H5 result. In one T08 trial (Qwen3.5-9B) the agent dropped orders_backup the same way. Injection following on MariaDB given exposure was 0.48 (26/54), in the range of the SQL engines in 5.5. The report accuracy measure of H6 was 0.254 [0.206, 0.309] over the 272 damaging trials on these engines. Full tables: Appendix A.4. 6. Mechanisms by engine The same mistake ends differently on different engines because of few mechanisms. Each is default or documented feature. None is measure of engine quality. 15 Cassandra. The shipped cassandra.yaml sets auto_snapshot: true, which takes snapshot before table is truncated or dropped [Cassandra-1][Cassandra-2]. TRUNCATE and DROP therefore leave copy that nodetool import can load back [Cassandra-3]. Least privilege does not stop TRUNCATE: the MODIFY permission covers INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE together [Cassandra-4]. So under G1 the statement succeeds, and the snapshot is what saves the data. Row deletes and updates leave no snapshot. In Layer B, this undid 82 of the 83 loss trials; the one permanent loss was an UPDATE. ClickHouse. In an Atomic database, dropped table stays in system.dropped_tables and UNDROP TABLE can bring it back within database_atomic_delay_before_drop_table_sec, 480 seconds by default, unless the drop used SYNC [ClickHouse-1][ClickHouse-2]. detached table can be attached again [ClickHouse-3]. Mutations cannot be rolled back once submitted [ClickHouse-4]. The documentation describes no undo for TRUNCATE or lightweight DELETE [ClickHouse-5][ClickHouse-6]. Lightweight DELETE requires the ALTER DELETE privilege [ClickHouse-6], while TRUNCATE and MODIFY TTL are separate privileges [ClickHouse-7]. Our least privilege granted ALTER DELETE and ALTER UPDATE, so it refused TRUNCATE and MODIFY TTL but still allowed lightweight DELETE and both mutations, which caused most of the remaining loss. In Layer B, the drill brought back dropped and detached tables, and 33 of the 83 loss trials whose replay matched kept their loss. PostgreSQL and SQLite. Both run most DDL, including DROP TABLE and (in PostgreSQL) TRUNCATE [PostgreSQL-7], inside transactions, so DROP TABLE inside an open transaction can be rolled back [PostgreSQL1][SQLite-1]; once committed, it cannot. PostgreSQL has exceptions, such as DROP DATABASE, which cannot run inside transaction block [PostgreSQL-6]. PostgreSQL archives WAL only when archive_mode is turned on, and it is off by default [PostgreSQL-2][PostgreSQL-3]. With base backup and archived WAL, the whole cluster, roles included, can be restored to point before the mistake [PostgreSQL-4][PostgreSQL-5]. SQLite has no users or GRANT [SQLite-2]; beyond file permissions it offers read-only open mode and an authorizer callback, which we did not test. Its backups are file copies, the backup API or VACUUM INTO [SQLite-3][SQLite-4]; our R1 copied the file while no connection was writing. There is no log to roll forward, so restore also loses legitimate writes made after the copy. MySQL and MariaDB. DDL and account statements commit any open transaction first, so BEGIN; DROP TABLE; ROLLBACK does not bring the table back [MySQL-1][MySQL-2][MariaDB-1]. MySQL has the binary log on by default, while MariaDB has it off unless the server starts with --log-bin [MySQL-3][MariaDB-2]. Point-in-time recovery restores dump and replays the binary log up to chosen position [MySQL-4][MariaDB-3]. That restores the dumped databases, but it does not return the servers accounts to the recovery point. dump of application databases holds no accounts. Even mysqldump --users --add-drop-user drops and recreates only the accounts in the dump [MySQL-5]. superuser created by the mistake therefore survives the recovery and must be removed by hand. Layer measured exactly this (M17 under R1, 4.3), with logical dump of the application databases restored onto the same server (mysqldump and mariadb-dump; [MariaDB-3] describes the same binary-log replay after mariadb-backup restore). We did not test physical backup or dump of the system schema. Kafka. topic deletion has no undo in the Admin API, and topic deletion is enabled by default [Kafka-1][Kafka-2]. Lowering retention.ms makes the broker discard older segments at its next retention check, by default within five minutes [Kafka-3][Kafka-4]. In the ACL model, deleting records and deleting topic need the same Topic Delete operation, and changing topic configuration needs AlterConfigs [Kafka-5]. Withholding those two removes all three paths, and the refusal reads Topic authorization failed [Kafka-6]. Our G1 (an ACL set of our own; Kafka documents producer and consumer ACL shortcuts but no recipe for an application role) withheld both, and permanent loss under G1 was 0 of 432 main-set trials. fourth path stays open under Write: producing newer record for key. Two main-set G0 trials and one subset G1 trial altered marker that way. Valkey. With only the default RDB snapshots on, FLUSHALL has no undo: in our measurement it wrote an empty dump.rdb at once. Prod data was in database 0, where connection starts; the system note told the agent so (9). After FLUSHDB the previous snapshot survives only until the next save point. AOF is off by default [Valkey-1][Valkey-2]. With AOF on, flush can be undone by removing the last command from the log before rewrite [Valkey-2]; separate smoke test of this R1 recipe outside Layer (AOF on, automatic rewrites off) restored the seeded state after FLUSHALL. Since 9.1, ACLs can restrict user to listed database numbers. user restricted that way cannot run FLUSHALL, which needs access to every database [Valkey-3][Valkey-4]. FLUSHDB inside an allowed database has to be withheld as command. Our G1 combined database restriction with withholding FLUSHDB, FLUSHALL and the @dangerous, @admin and @scripting categories; permanent loss under 16 G1 was 1 of 432. MongoDB. The built-in readWrite role includes dropCollection [MongoDB-1]. least-privilege identity that must not drop collections therefore needs custom role built from privilege actions [MongoDB-2]. mongorestore --oplogReplay replays dumped oplog after restore, and --oplogLimit stops the replay at timestamp; MongoDB warns that setting this limit by hand might cause corruption and inconsistencies. mongodump --oplog captures only the entries written during the dump [MongoDB-3][MongoDB-4]. We did not drill an oplog replay. OpenSearch. action.destructive_requires_name defaults to false in OpenSearch, so wildcard such as DELETE /staging-* deletes every matching index [OpenSearch-1][OpenSearch-2]. Elasticsearch has defaulted it to true since 8.0 [Elasticsearch-1][Elasticsearch-2]. Index deletion is the action indices:admin/delete, which the manage and indices_all action groups include and crud does not [OpenSearch-3][OpenSearch-4]. Recovery needs registered snapshot repository, and none exists by default [OpenSearch-5]. 7. What an operator can change 1. Turn on the vendors minimum backup with its change log where the engine has one (R1). In Layer this removed every loss of protected rows on all four relational engines (on MySQL and MariaDB, check the accounts separately, 4.3). 2. Do not keep backup inside the same namespace and under the same identity the agent uses: out of the box, more than half of the loss trials lost only such copy, in T08 and in the free-space task T02. 3. Give the agent the vendors least-privilege identity, and where the engine allows it, withhold the destructive operation itself. Withholding flushes on Valkey and topic and record deletion on Kafka removed the loss of original rows there; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse, where row deletes and mutations stay allowed, most original-row loss came from deletes G1 allows (the injected instruction in T04, and DELETE where TRUNCATE was refused), so it stayed about the same. 4. denylist in front of the database can complement least privilege, not replace it; ours was tested only against mistakes written alongside it, and its published bypasses defeat it. 5. Do not trust the agents report to find what to restore. Diff the state. 6. Expect the agent to try other identities when refused: default superuser credentials must not work, and no credential should be stored where the agent can read it (5.3). 8. sections.title: Effect
sections.content: Further scorer pattern gaps recounted from raw records: attempted-damage verbs, H6 false positives, delayed-damage and refusal patterns, the unmatched ClickHouse replay, Valkeys default database (S13) Preregistered secondary outcome exfiltration into the output channel was never implemented Human audit planned before the runs is not reported: how the two rating sheets were completed was not documented well enough to treat them as independent human labels Applicability review (amendment v2: blind review by two reviewers) described as review by two of the authors descriptive; preregistered counts kept one secondary outcome not reported no reported number depends on it; the scorer has no human validation none on any number The preregistered outcome permanent loss after the engine-native drill was always the primary outcome, but Layer as run stored no drill result: its in-run recovery step did nothing. For seven engines this changes nothing (no in-engine undo in R0). For ClickHouse and Cassandra the drill was reconstructed by replay after the first tables, and the analysis plan first declared their measured loss an upper bound. Their headline results (including Cassandras 0 of 432) therefore rest on an analysis added after the tables. The raw loss for those engines is reported next to the drilled loss (5.1). The preregistration also fixed the pairing unit for G0 vs G1 (the task instance) but not the test; the trial-level McNemar tests come from the analysis plan and are less conservative than the post-hoc instance-level tests, which use the preregistered unit (S2), and the template-level tests (S8, S11), which cannot reach significance with about dozen templates per engine. 9. Limitations Attempted damage is detected by statement patterns (layer-b/score.ts). The patterns count any delete or update, including the ones task asked for, and they miss some destructive forms on the engines the models used least well (MongoDB shell write methods such as deleteMany, remove and updateOne, OpenSearch _update_by_query, invented Kafka operation names). H4 should be read with both in mind (5.2). Valkeys previous snapshot and default database. After FLUSHDB the previous RDB file survives until the next save point, but in our harness it was usually the empty file written by FLUSHALL when the server was reset before each trial, so restoring it would not have helped; on long-running server it could, and Valkeys figures would then be lower. Our Valkey layout put prod data in database 0, where every connection starts, so FLUSHDB meant for staging that skipped SELECT 1 removed prod data; on the SQL engines the agents session did not open inside the prod data, so the same slip would have failed. The same applies to Redis in the extended run (one database, prefixes). Models. Six small open-weight models, 4-bit quantised, on one machine. Frontier models and commercial agent products were not tested. We use the models to generate realistic mistakes, and we make claims about engines and configurations, not about models in general. Clustered trials. The preregistered intervals and McNemar tests treat trials as independent, but outcomes repeat across seeds and each engine has only 36 task instances. Instance-level analyses (5.1, Appendix A.2) are wider, and several G1 effects do not survive them. The backup copy. Out of the box, more than half of the loss trials lost only the backup copy, whose originals survive (5.1). The preregistered outcome counts it; the loss of original rows is reported next to it. 19 Competence. On Kafka, MongoDB and Valkey, the models often could not use the interface (5.6), so Layer under-samples skilled misuse on these engines. Layer covers four engines. Mechanisms on the other engines come from Layer and vendor documentation. Replay drill. The drill ran seconds after the replayed statements, while in the original trial up to the trials length had passed (ClickHouse keeps dropped tables for 480 s). The replay reproduces only statements that succeeded. Statements that read the clock produce different values. R1 on SQLite is file copy taken after seeding. In this world nothing legitimate happens after seeding, so it restores fully; in production it would lose the writes since the copy. Data plane only. Many real incidents happened in the platform layer (cloud APIs, infrastructure as code, volume deletion), which this study does not measure. Single-node, default-sized engines with small synthetic dataset. Replication, managed services and their provider-specific defaults are out of scope. No human validation of the scorer. The human audit planned before the runs is not reported (8). The scorer was checked against the raw records by the authors and by AI-model reviews the authors ran. Reading transcripts found one blind spot of the canary design (non-canary prod deletions in an in-scope object, 5.8); the reviews found the pattern gaps below. Pattern-based scorer flags. Several secondary flags match statement or setting text and missed or over-counted cases, found by those reviews and recounted from the raw records (post hoc, S12-S13): the planted-credential flag on Cassandra, injection soft deletes, key-value and document updates in the attempted-damage measure, accurate reports flagged as misstating, TTL settings of 0 flagged as delayed damage, and failed logins counted as refusals. The preregistered outcome (canary loss from the state difference) does not depend on these patterns; one Valkey loss is most likely harness artefact (5.1). 10. Ethics, conflict of interest and funding The study was designed, run and funded by the team behind LibreDB Studio, an open-source (MIT) database tool. The same team also offers commercial product, LibreDB Platform; it played no part in the study. LibreDB Studio is listed, unpaid, on community or ecosystem pages of several projects in the study. We have no commercial relationship with any engine vendor or model provider in the study. LibreDBs own agent is not part of any arm; the read-only list_objects tool is built on LibreDB Studios provider layer and is identical in every arm. LibreDBs MCP tool derives read-only behaviour from the engines own read-only path, which aligns with one possible outcome of H2. We disclosed this in the preregistration. Following the Jepsen model, every vendor and model provider received the draft on 1 November 2026 with 21 days to reply. No reply reported factual error and none was an official statement; corrections that arrive later will be published as new version. All data is synthetic and local.
